div.p: Sent you a few days ago the Nausikaa episode. Will you please forward it at once to Miss Weaver and to New York. They write (N.Y.) that the instalments are all due. Am starting on Oxen of the Sun .

div.note: The face of this postcard reproduces a watercolor captioned “VENEZIA – Sul Molo.” The artist is Gian Luciano Sormani (1867-1938), born in Legnano, Italy, and a student of Pompeo Molmenti (1819-1894). Sormani was a painter and bookbinder who settled in Venice and was known for pencil-and-watercolor scenes of Venetian lagoon daily life (Benezit Dictionary of Artists, Oxford Art Online). His work appeared on numerous postcards produced by Stabilimento Litografico A. Scrocchi, a lithography publishing company founded by Attilio Scrocchi around 1880 in Milan. The painting is of the Molo, the celebrated stone quay in Venice, with a view of part of the Doge’s Palace and the base of St. Mark’s column. The Molo offers some of the most popular views in Venice and has been painted by countless artists, perhaps most famously Canaletto (1697-1768). The postcard image may have been JJ’s response to the fact that the Pounds were considering a visit to Venice and other parts of Italy in the spring, as Pound wrote his mother on 14 January 1920 (Ezra Pound to his Parents: Letters 1885-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 459). JJ himself had never been to Venice at this point in his life (see JJ to Pound, 18 May 1920), but in early July 1920 he stopped there for two days on his way to Paris (Ellmann, JJ 482).

JJ sent two typed copies of “Nausicaa,” the thirteenth episode of Ulysses, to Pound in London circa 2-4 February 1920 (LI 137). Pound forwarded one of these to New York for serialization in The Little Review (Pound/Joyce 173). “Nausicaa” appeared in three numbers of The Little Review, vol. 6, no. 11-vol. 7, nos. 1-2 (April, May-June, July-August 1920): 43-50, 61-72, 42-58. The portion in the July-August 1920 number, containing the scene of Leopold Bloom’s masturbation at the seashore, caused the editors Margaret Caroline Anderson (1886-1973) and Jane Heap (1883-1964) to be prosecuted for publishing obscenity; they were convicted and fined $50 each by a New York court in 1921. As soon as he read the typescript of “Nausicaa” in London, Pound was aware that the episode risked censorship. He told JJ that he had renamed it “Bloom by the sea waves & the lady of delectable shins” (Pound/Joyce 173). More frankly, he wrote John Quinn on 21 February 1920 that the episode had an “excellent start but think [JJ] gets a bit too too too at the end of it [where Bloom ejaculates in his pants]. Have suggested slight alterations, but see perfectly well that if every possible physical secretion is to be affichéd [displayed, flaunted] in course of the work, even this calamity must happen to Mr. Bloom. Perhaps everything ought to be said ONCE in the English language[.] At least J. seems bent on saying it. Who am I to tamper with a work of genius. For bigod genius it is in parts” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 185). For fuller accounts of “Nausicaa” and the prosecution and trial it occasioned, see JJ to Pound, 24 October 1919, notes; 5 November 1920, notes; and 16 November 1920, notes.

As JJ completed episodes of Ulysses, he had copies typed and sent to Pound, who reviewed and transmitted them to New York for serial publication in The Little Review, and to Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961), editor of The Egoist in London. Because of English printers’ fears, The Egoist never consistently serialized Ulysses, and published only a few episodes: “Nestor,” “Proteus,” “Hades,” and part of “Wandering Rocks.”

“Oxen of the Sun,” the fourteenth episode of Ulysses, takes place in the Maternity Hospital in Dublin, where some medical students, Stephen Dedalus, and a few others are carousing. Leopold Bloom joins the group but avoids alcohol. The episode progresses by a chronological series of literary styles beginning with what JJ called a “Sallustian-Tacitean prelude (the unfertilized ovum),” proceeding through pastiches of Anglo-Saxon alliteration, Middle English romance, Elizabethan chronicle, and “Defoe-Swift and Steele-Addison-Sterne and Landor-Pater-Newman,” and ending in “a frightful jumble of Pidgin English, nigger English, Cockney, Irish, Bowery slang and broken doggerel” – the whole being suggestive, JJ claimed, of “the natural stages of development in the embryo and the periods of faunal evolution in general” (LI 139-40). The rowdy drinkers disturb the resident patients with their clamor about contraception, pregnancy, abortion, and motherhood. The Homeric parallel links these irreverent roisterers to Odysseus’s crew who, in Book 12 of The Odyssey, break a solemn oath by slaughtering the sacred cattle of the sun-god Helios to furnish forth a feast to break their famine, after which crew and ship are destroyed by Zeus. Odysseus alone, like sober Bloom, survives the wreck. Pound received “Oxen of the Sun” from JJ and forwarded it to The Little Review, referring to the episode as “Feast in House of Horne,” that is, Dr. Andrew Horne, master of the Maternity Hospital (Pound/Joyce 173). After the first pages of “Oxen of the Sun” had appeared in The Little Review, vol. 7, no. 3 (September-December 1920): 81-92, the magazine’s editors were convicted of publishing obscenity (the portion of “Nausicaa” in the July-August 1920 number), and the serialization of Ulysses ended.
